newsitem.title: USA: U.S. researchers warn of iron deficiencies.
newsitem.headline: U.S. researchers warn of iron deficiencies.

text.p: Iron deficiency and resulting anemia remained a serious problem for many young children, adolescent girls and women of childbearing age in the United States, researchers said on Tuesday.

Despite successful U.S. efforts in the past three decades to combat blood iron deficiency levels by introducing iron-fortified infant formula and foods, an estimated 9 percent of children 1 to 2 years old were found to be iron deficient in a study that covered 1988 to 1994.
The National Center for Health Statistics, part of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in Hyattsville, Maryland, studied data on nearly 25,000 people ages 1 year and older.

"The prevalences observed in this study translate into 7.8 million adolescent girls and women of childbearing age with iron deficiency; of these, approximately 3.3 million have iron deficiency anemia," study author Anne Looker wrote in the Journal of the American Medical Association.
"Estimates for toddlers show approximately 700,000 with iron deficiency and approximately 240,000 of these with iron deficiency anemia," she wrote.

A deficiency of iron in the blood combined with low levels of hemoglobin can cause anemia, harm the functioning of the immune system, slow down cognitive development and damage the body's ability to regulate temperature and energy metabolism.

The study found that iron deficiency was twice as high or greater among minority women compared to white women, and was more common among poor women, those with less education and those with more children. Women over age 50 were not as likely as younger women to be iron deficient, but were still more likely to lack iron than men, the study found.
